name: Luna 3
short_status: Looped behind the Moon and photographed the far side on 7 Oct 1959; 17 of 29 film frames were received by 18 Oct, and contact was lost 22 Oct 1959.
tagline: OKB-1 · Soviet Union · Flyby · 1959 · The space race Success
stats: film frames of the never-before-seen far side
usable images radioed back to Earth
of photography that redrew the Moon

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 4 October 1959, 00:43:40 UT, Tyuratam (Baikonur), on an 8K72 (no. I1-8)

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: 278.5 kg Ye-2A 'Automatic Interplanetary Station'; 130 cm long, 120 cm max diameter; solar cells, spin-stabilized, gas-jet attitude control

facts.label: Trajectory
facts.value: Highly elliptical Earth orbit of ~48,280 x 468,300 km; passed the Moon's south polar region and returned over the north

facts.label: Closest approach
facts.value: 6,200 km above the surface, 6 October 1959 at 14:16 UT (NSSDCA); sources giving ~7,900 km (NASA's retired page, citing Siddiqi) measure from the Moon's center, which minus the ~1,737 km lunar radius matches NSSDCA

facts.label: Photography
facts.value: 7 October 1959, first frame 03:30 UT at 63,500 km, last frame 40 minutes later at 66,700 km; 29 frames covering ~70% of the far side

facts.label: Camera
facts.value: Yenisey-2 dual-lens system (200 mm f/5.6 and 500 mm f/9.5), 40-frame 35 mm radiation-resistant film, onboard develop/fix/dry, CRT scanner up to 1,000 lines

facts.label: Film provenance (reported)
facts.value: Film designated ASh-1, reportedly recovered from downed American Genetrix reconnaissance balloons

facts.label: Images returned
facts.value: 17 resolvable but noisy photographs received by 18 October 1959; contact lost 22 October

facts.label: Fate
facts.value: Believed to have burned up in Earth's atmosphere in March or April 1960; may have survived in orbit until after 1962

facts.label: Naming legacy
facts.value: Mare Moscoviense and crater Tsiolkovskiy named from these images; 'Mare Desiderii' later found to be a composite and dropped

timeline: Launch at 00:43:40 UT from Tyuratam (Baikonur), two years to the day after Sputnik 1
14:16 UT: Closest approach: 6,200 km above the surface (about 7,900 km from the Moon's center) over the south polar region
03:30 UT: First photograph of the lunar far side, taken from 63,500 km; 29 frames follow over 40 minutes
First transmission attempts fail due to weak signal at long range
17 resolvable but noisy photographs received as the spacecraft nears Earth
Believed to have burned up in Earth's atmosphere (NSSDCA notes it may have survived in orbit past 1962)
